title: Febrile convulsion: counselling
stem: Paediatric observation ward. Lok-yin, 20 months, had a 2-minute generalised seizure at home with a temperature of 39.5 °C. He is now alert, playing, with a viral URTI and no other findings. His parents are frightened. Explain what happened and advise them.
notes:
Checked against the NICE CKS (Febrile seizure, 2023), AAP 2011 clinical practice guideline on simple febrile seizures, and RCPCH guidance.

Simple febrile seizure: age 6 months to 5 years, generalised, under 15 minutes, not recurring within 24 hours, complete recovery within an hour, with fever and no CNS infection. Complex: focal, over 15 minutes, recurrent within 24 hours, or incomplete recovery — needs more assessment. Look for the cause of the fever and for signs of meningitis (a lower threshold for LP in infants under 12 months, those pretreated with antibiotics, or with incomplete immunisation). Simple febrile seizures need no EEG or imaging and do not cause brain damage. Recurrence about 30% (higher if first under 18 months, family history, low fever at seizure, short fever before seizure); risk of later epilepsy about 1–2% (slightly above the population). Antipyretics make the child comfortable but do not prevent recurrence. Seizure first aid: recovery position, time it, nothing in the mouth; call an ambulance if over 5 minutes; buccal midazolam only if prescribed for prolonged seizures.

Your notes list paediatric seizure as a topic; nothing conflicts.

Event.r: His whole body stiffened then jerked for about 2 minutes. Sleepy for 20 minutes, then fine.

Event.t: Did it affect one side more? Another seizure since?
Event.r: Both sides the same. Only one.

Background.r: Up to date. His father had fits with fevers as a toddler.

steps.label: Explain and advise
steps.hint: What it is, not epilepsy, no brain damage, recurrence, what to do next time, fever care.

turns.line: I thought he was dying. Has it damaged his brain?

opts.t: That must have been terrifying. This was a febrile convulsion — a fit triggered by a fever. It happens in about 1 in 30 young children and doesn't cause brain damage.
opts.mark: Acknowledges fear and explains febrile convulsions and no brain damage

turns.line: Is it epilepsy? Will it happen again?

opts.t: It's not epilepsy. About 1 in 3 children have another with a future fever, usually before age 5. The chance of later epilepsy is only slightly higher than other children.
opts.r: What should we do if it happens again?

turns.line: What should we do if it happens again?

opts.t: Lay him on his side on a safe surface, time it, put nothing in his mouth. If it lasts over 5 minutes, call an ambulance. Paracetamol or ibuprofen make him comfortable but don't prevent fits, so don't wake him at night for them.
opts.mark: Seizure first aid and correct advice on antipyretics

opts.t: Give paracetamol every 4 hours around the clock to prevent fits.

qs.a: Focal onset or duration over 15 minutes

wrong: Only if given round the clock
